description: An all-female, USA-based team of high school students and first-year college students interested in computer engineering. This was each team member's first year in the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Our project, Submicron, is a data visualization website that ranks NASA microgravity combustion investigations (SAME, SAME-R, Saffire I-VI, DAFT, BASS, and FLEX) by fire detection performance.
summary:
Submicron ranks NASA's microgravity combustion investigations by fire detection performance, a factor most fire safety work treats separately from the combustion science itself. In microgravity, smoke does not rise. It travels with ventilation airflow, and its particle size decides whether a detector can see it at all.

We scored six investigations (SAME, SAME-R, Saffire I-VI, DAFT, BASS, and FLEX) on detector testing, particle characterization, detection speed evidence, environment match, and scale, using published NASA and NIST data. In the SAME experiments, the ISS photoelectric detector failed to alarm for Kapton smoke in half of tests and Teflon smoke in two thirds.

The site turns that scoring into visualization. Visitors can compare any two studies by detection speed, check which materials on a vehicle fall in a fitted detector's blind spot, and visualize measured smoke particle data.
details:
Submicron is a data analysis and visualization tool that compares six NASA microgravity combustion investigations (SAME, SAME-R, Saffire I-VI, DAFT, BASS, and FLEX) on fire detection performance. These investigations were not designed as detection studies, and NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database stores each one separately, with no cross-investigation comparison. Submicron extracts the detection variables from the published records and reports into a common schema: materials burned, smoke particle size measurements, detector types tested, alarm outcomes, test environment, and experiment scale. Each investigation is scored on: detector testing (30 points), detection speed evidence (25), particle characterization (20), environment match (15), and scale (10). Scores are computed only from published values. In the SAME flight data, the ISS photoelectric detector produced no alarm for Kapton smoke in 1 of 2 tests and for Teflon smoke in 2 of 3 tests, and measured mean smoke particle diameters were 100 to 200 nm across materials. These rules below are original to this project, PSI provides none of them. The dataset is presented through four interfaces. Understanding Smoke Detection reports a categorical verdict for each material against the ISS detector: detected, detection gap, or insufficient published data. Compare Speed renders a slope chart of two selected investigations across the rubric components and ranks all six by the speed evidence component. Compare Materials evaluates a user-selected set of vehicle materials against a selected detector (ISS photoelectric, Shuttle ionization, or dual technology) and reports which materials fall inside that detector's measured insensitivity range. The Investigations page re-ranks all six under four environment models (ISS, lunar surface at elevated oxygen, rover, Mars transit) using fixed adjustment rules stated on the page. The particle size chart plots detector response against particle diameter on a logarithmic axis from 10 to 10,000 nm. The measured SAME distributions are drawn at their published values: mean band 100 to 200 nm, a substantial fraction below 500 nm, Teflon primarily below 1,000 nm. The detector response curves carry no numeric values, because NASA and NIST publish no sensitivity-by-diameter table. Detector and material selection for future spacecraft and surface habitats currently requires reading each investigation report separately. Submicron reduces that to a direct comparison, and it identifies a measured result with design consequences. Teflon and Kapton, the two materials with a recorded detection gap, are both used as insulation around spacecraft electronics.

Factors considered: 1. data limits, no per-material time-to-alarm values are published, so detection speed is scored from transport and aging measurements instead of invented alarm times (SAME smoke aging range 10 to 1800 seconds; in Saffire-V, a 0.66 mg/m3 particulate increase recorded 57 seconds after an airflow change from 0 to 20 cm/s). 2. detector physics, photoelectric detectors respond weakly to submicron particles and ionization detectors respond weakly to large particles, and the material verdicts follow from this and from the SAME alarm record. 3. false alarms, DAFT measured dust with the same instrument as SAME and is included as the control case for smoke versus dust discrimination.
